message.content:
**Pantone “sky‑blue” – common choices**

| # | Description / Usage | Typical Pantone Code |
|---|---------------------|----------------------|
| **A** | *Very pale, almost pastel* – often used as a background or accent in print & web design. | **Pantone 290 C** |
| **B** | *Bright, cheerful sky‑blue* – popular in branding, apparel, and packaging. | **Pantone 292 C** |
| **C** | *Softer, slightly muted tone* – good for corporate stationery where you don’t want an overly bright hue. | **Pantone 293 C** |
| **D** | *Standard “sky blue” from many style guides* – frequently cited in interior décor palettes. | **Pantone 295 C** |

> **Why there’s more than one:**  
> - Pantone has dozens of blues that all fall under the umbrella term “sky.”  
> - Different industries pick different ones based on how saturated or matte/metallic they prefer.  

### Quick guide to picking the right one:

| Need | Recommended Choice | Why it works |
|------|--------------------|--------------|
| Lightest, most airy feel | Pantone 290 C | Very low saturation → feels open and fresh. |
| Bright, eye‑catching | Pantone 292 C | Higher saturation gives vibrancy without being too intense. |
| Subtle, professional look | Pantone 293 C | Slightly deeper but still soft enough for business use. |
| Classic “sky blue” reference | Pantone 295 C | Often referenced in textbooks and design standards. |

---

#### How to verify your choice

If you’re working with a printer or designer who uses physical swatches:
1. Grab a Pantone® Color Bridge Guide or a Pantone™ Matching System book.  
2. Look up each of the above codes—most will show both CMYK values and a printed sample so you know exactly what the ink looks like.

For digital work, convert the chosen Pantone to RGB/HSL via Adobe Illustrator or online converters. Keep in mind that screen displays may render the color slightly differently due to gamut differences.

Feel free to let me know which context you’re designing for (print, UI, textiles), and I can narrow down the best match!
